演奏西奧爾博琴時，右手以撥弦或掃弦發聲，左手在指板上按弦。初學先讀指法譜，其上平: To play the theorbo, the right hand plucks or strums to make the sound and the left hand stops the strings on the fingerboard. A beginner first reads tablature, in which the parallel lines stand for the strings and the figures mark the fret and string to be stopped. The tuning is re-entrant, with the top two strings an octave lower, so chords are laid out differently from those of an ordinary lute. The right hand may use thumb, index and middle finger for arpeggios; in continuo accompaniment the bass sometimes has to be played an octave lower to keep the bass line clear. French writings also mention using a chord whose bass note sounds later when the bass is too high.

西奧爾博琴於十六世紀末在義大利發展，因佛羅倫斯卡梅拉塔的歌劇與通奏低音需要更低音: The theorbo developed in Italy at the end of the sixteenth century, called for by the operas of the Florentine Camerata and by the continuo's need for a lower range. Early on a large bass lute had its neck lengthened and a second pegbox added, with open bass strings, improving clarity and range. In the Baroque period (1600–1750) it was used for continuo and for solo playing, often together with the organ, and it spread to England, France and Germany: England mostly used a G tuning and double strings and replaced it with the bowed lute after the eighteenth century; in France it is recorded in 1637 and had become an important accompanying instrument by the 1660s; Germany developed the swan-neck Baroque lute and the theorbo-lute.
西奧爾博琴是撥弦樂器，屬弦鳴，起源於義大利與地中海地區。來源顯示它在巴洛克時期用: The theorbo is a plucked instrument of the chordophones, originating in Italy and the Mediterranean. The source shows it used for continuo accompaniment in the Baroque period, usually alongside the harpsichord, organ and bass instruments, and also as a solo instrument; it also appears in the accompaniment of early opera and monody, and both Caccini's 'Le nuove musiche' and Monteverdi's 'Orfeo' mention the instrument. It was also used by English consort and opera orchestras, by French court orchestras or chamber music, and by the court orchestras of Vienna, Bayreuth and Berlin; German sources say it suits ensembles of thirty to forty players in church and opera.
西奧爾博琴是魯特琴家族的撥弦樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 321: The theorbo is a plucked instrument of the lute family, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-5. It has a lengthened neck and a second pegbox, a soundbox with a curved back and a flat soundboard, and usually one or three soundholes with a rose. The player plucks or strums with the right hand and stops with the left. Its range is close to the cello's, and in the Baroque it was mostly used for continuo accompaniment in opera, at court and in chamber music, and also as a solo instrument.
西奧爾博琴為撥弦樂器，以右手撥或掃弦、左手按弦發聲；其長頸與第二弦軸箱容納較長的: The theorbo is a plucked instrument, sounding when the right hand plucks or strums and the left stops the strings; its long neck and second pegbox carry the longer open bass strings, which makes the bass clearer and extends the range, overall close to the cello's. The tuning is re-entrant, with the top two strings an octave lower, which suits harmonic progressions and the bass part; Piccinini compared the right hand's arpeggios with thumb, index and middle finger to the sound of a harp. Its volume varies with the type and the ensemble; in continuo it is usually paired with the organ and the like; Baron said its power suits large church and opera ensembles, while the lute better suits a trio. The French type is smaller and quieter, and the English type mostly has double strings with only the first string an octave lower.
西奧爾博琴為撥弦樂器，來源僅明確記載弦材：部分文獻提及金屬弦（黃銅、鋼）與腸弦；: The theorbo is a plucked instrument, and the source records only the string material clearly: some writings mention metal strings (brass, steel) and gut strings; the materials of the body, soundboard, fingerboard, pegs and other parts are not stated. Its sounding body is the strings, set going by the right hand's pluck or strum and stopped by the left; the soundbox is flat-topped with a curved back and usually has one or three soundholes decorated with a rose, but the source does not say what these parts are made of.
